los.text: Describe the signs, symptoms and main causes of inflammatory joint disease (focus on gout)
los.html:
• Gout: monosodium urate crystal deposition when serum urate exceeds saturation (~0.36–0.40 mmol/L).
Cause of hyperuricaemiaExamples
↓ Renal excretion (~90%)CKD, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin, alcohol, dehydration, lead
↑ Production: dietRed meat, offal, seafood, beer/spirits, fructose drinks
↑ Production: cell turnoverMyeloproliferative disorders, psoriasis, tumour lysis, HGPRT deficiency
Risk factorsMale, age, obesity, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, CKD, FHx.
Acute attack
  • Rapid onset (overnight, peaks in 24 h) exquisitely painful, red, hot, swollen joint
  • 1st MTP (podagra) ~50%, also ankle, midfoot, knee, wrist
  • Triggers: alcohol binge, dehydration, trauma, surgery, starting urate-lowering therapy.
  • May have low-grade fever.
Chronic tophaceous goutTophi (ears, fingers, olecranon bursa, Achilles), chronic arthritis with erosions, urate nephropathy and stones.
Pseudogout (CPPD)Older patients, knee/wrist; positively birefringent rhomboid crystals; chondrocalcinosis.
A hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise: aspirate.

los.text: Describe the investigations and principles of treatment / management of gout
sessions: Clin 2: Gout pathophysiology, diagnosis and management
los.html:
DiagnosisJoint aspiration → polarised light microscopy: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals (gold standard); also Gram stain and culture to exclude sepsis.
Serum urateCan be normal during an attack; recheck ≥2 weeks after the flare.
Other bloodsU&E (CKD), CRP/WCC (raised), glucose/lipids (CV risk).
Imaging
  • X-ray in chronic gout: punched-out juxta-articular erosions with overhanging edges, preserved joint space until late, soft-tissue tophi.
  • USS (double contour sign) and dual-energy CT for urate.
Acute management
  • Rest, elevate, ice.
  • NSAID (+ PPI) or colchicine (renal dose adjustment)
  • Oral prednisolone or intra-articular steroid if both contraindicated.
  • Don't stop established allopurinol during a flare.
Long-term (BSR/NICE)
  • Offer urate-lowering therapy (ULT) to all with gout, especially if recurrent flares, tophi, CKD, diuretic use, stones.
  • Treat-to-target serum urate <0.36 mmol/L (<0.30 if tophi/frequent flares).
  • Start ~2–4 weeks after flare settles (or during, with cover), titrate monthly.
  • Flare prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine (or NSAID) for ~6 months when starting ULT.
Lifestyle
  • Weight loss, reduce alcohol (especially beer), avoid sugary drinks and high-purine foods, hydrate
  • Switch thiazide to losartan (uricosuric) if possible
  • Review aspirin.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat gout and septic arthritis and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
DrugMechanismKey points
NSAIDs (naproxen)COX inhibitionAcute flares; avoid in CKD, PUD, HF; give PPI
ColchicineInhibits microtubule polymerisation → ↓ neutrophil migration/activation, ↓ NLRP3 inflammasome500 μg BD–QDS (max 6 mg/course); diarrhoea; toxic in renal impairment; interactions (clarithromycin, statins via CYP3A4/P-gp)
CorticosteroidsAnti-inflammatoryOral prednisolone 30–35 mg 5 days, or IA injection
Allopurinol (1st-line ULT)Xanthine oxidase inhibitor → ↓ urate production
  • Start 100 mg (lower in CKD), titrate to target.
  • Rash → stop (DRESS/SJS; HLA-B*5801 in Han Chinese, Thai, Korean).
  • Azathioprine/mercaptopurine interaction (↑ toxicity)
FebuxostatNon-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor2nd line; caution in CVD
Uricosurics (benzbromarone, probenecid)↓ renal tubular urate reabsorption (URAT1)Specialist; avoid with stones
Pegloticase/rasburicaseRecombinant uricase → urate to allantoinRefractory gout / tumour lysis
  • Septic arthritis (empirical, BNF/local): aspirate first, then IV flucloxacillin (S. aureus)
    • clindamycin if penicillin-allergic
    • vancomycin if MRSA
    • ceftriaxone if gonococcal or gram-negative risk (elderly, IVDU).
    • Typically IV ~2 weeks then oral to total 4–6 weeks
    • joint washout (arthroscopic/open) and repeated aspiration.
    • Prosthetic joint infection → orthopaedics.

los.text: Describe the processes of musculoskeletal connective tissue repair and regeneration following injury/disease (include current strategies in tissue engineering)
sessions: BMS 1: Tissue engineering and cartilage repair
los.html:
Healing capacity varies with blood supply and cell turnover
  • Bone (excellent: regeneration without scar)
  • Muscle (satellite cells; large injuries → fibrosis)
  • Tendon/ligament (slow, scar-like, type III collagen → remodelled)
  • Articular cartilage (very poor: avascular, chondrocytes trapped in matrix; partial-thickness defects don't heal; full-thickness defects reaching bone → marrow cells → fibrocartilage, mechanically inferior)
  • Meniscus (outer red zone heals, inner white zone doesn't).
Current cartilage repair strategies
  • Marrow stimulation (microfracture): drill subchondral bone → clot with MSCs → fibrocartilage. Cheap; deteriorates over years.
  • Osteochondral autograft (mosaicplasty) / allograft: transfer plugs of bone + hyaline cartilage.
  • Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI/MACI): harvest cartilage → expand chondrocytes in lab → implant under a membrane/on a scaffold (NICE-approved for selected knee defects).
Tissue engineering triadCells (chondrocytes, mesenchymal stem cells, iPSCs) + scaffolds (collagen, hyaluronan, synthetic polymers, hydrogels, 3D-printed) + signals (growth factors: TGF-β, BMPs, IGF-1; mechanical stimulation in bioreactors).
Other approachesPRP injections (limited evidence), gene therapy, bone grafts/BMPs for non-union, tendon augmentation scaffolds.
ChallengesIntegration with host tissue, recreating zonal structure, durability, cost, regulation.

los.text: Explain the key theoretical and clinical explanations of stress and how they inform its management and treatment
los.html:
StressState when demands are perceived to exceed resources.
Theories
  • Fight or flight (Cannon): sympathetic–adrenal medullary activation (adrenaline).
  • General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye): alarm → resistance → exhaustion; chronic HPA axis activation (cortisol) → immune suppression, hypertension, metabolic effects.
  • Life events (Holmes & Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale): cumulative life changes predict illness. Criticised (ignores individual appraisal). Daily hassles may matter more.
  • Transactional model (Lazarus & Folkman): primary appraisal (threat? harm? challenge?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?) → stress response. Explains individual differences.
  • Allostatic load (McEwen): cumulative physiological wear and tear.
  • Demand–control model (Karasek) for work stress; effort–reward imbalance.
ModeratorsSocial support (buffering), personality (hardiness, type A hostility), sense of control, coping style.
EffectsAnxiety, depression, poor sleep, ↑ CVD risk, ↓ immunity (slower wound healing), unhealthy behaviours (smoking, alcohol, eating).
Management
  • Problem-focused coping (change the situation) and emotion-focused coping (change the response)
  • CBT/stress inoculation training, relaxation, mindfulness-based stress reduction, exercise, social support, organisational changes (workload, control)
  • Medication only for associated disorders.
